facts.statement: The genus contains only one species, S. pfisterae, which is known from a partial skeleton.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, S. pfisterae, known from a partial skeleton.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen, GPM5001, was discovered at the Old Woman Anticline in 1995 and is now held by the Paleon Museum in Glenrock.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, GPM5001, was found at the Old Woman Anticline in the upper Pierre Shale in 1995 and brought to the collection of the Paleon Museum in Glenrock.

facts.statement: The fossil material includes a partial skull, lower jaw, vertebral column, left ilium, and pubis.
facts.quote: It consists of a partial skull, lower jaw, and vertebral column, in addition to the left ilium and pubis.

facts.statement: The generic name Serpentisuchops combines Latin words for snake and crocodile with a Greek word for face.
facts.quote: The generic name, "Serpentisuchops", is derived from the Latin words "serpens", meaning "snake", and "suchus" meaning "crocodile", and the Greek word "ops", meaning "face".

facts.statement: The specific name pfisterae honors Anna Pfister, the landowner where the holotype was found.
facts.quote: The specific name, "pfisterae", honors Anna Pfister, on whose land the holotype was discovered.

facts.statement: Serpentisuchops is a medium-sized plesiosaur that reaches over 7 meters in total body length.
facts.quote: Serpentisuchops is a medium-sized plesiosaur, reaching over 7 m in total body length.

facts.statement: Serpentisuchops is unusual among derived plesiosaurs because it possesses both a long snout and a long neck.
facts.quote: It is unusual among derived plesiosaurs, as it has both a long snout and long neck.

facts.statement: The long snout of Serpentisuchops is likely an ancestral trait, while its long neck is a secondarily derived feature convergent with other groups.
facts.quote: The long snout of Serpentisuchops was likely an ancestral trait, while the long neck was secondarily derived and convergent with ancestral plesiosaurs, contemporary elasmosaurids, and some more basal members of the Polycotylidae.

facts.statement: The time range for Serpentisuchops is the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)
